strengths: Addresses an important scalability bottleneck in amortized causal discovery with a concrete architecture that combines a reduction unit, tied attention weights, and a two-stream data/graph design.
Demonstrates training on graphs up to 500 nodes and inference on graphs up to 1000 nodes, with reported speedups over several baselines (e.g., 0.83s vs 10,896s for NOTEARS at n=1000).

Includes a reasonably broad experimental suite: synthetic SCMs with multiple mechanisms, SERGIO-GRN data, OOD graph/noise/function settings, multiple metrics (mAP, SHD, AUC, OA), and ablations for the reduction unit, graph prior/stream, attention tying, prediction head, and pooling strategy.
Provides an efficiency analysis of the reduction unit and tied attention, with clear asymptotic memory savings for attention maps (O(RHC^2) to O(HC^2)).
The impact statement is appropriately cautious, framing predicted graphs as hypotheses to be validated rather than definitive causal conclusions.
weaknesses: The inverse covariance graph prior is mathematically ill-defined for the n=1000 synthetic setting: with m=1000 samples and n=1000 variables, the empirical covariance matrix is rank deficient and cannot be inverted as written. The paper does not state any regularization, shrinkage, or pseudo-inverse, so the headline n=1000 results are not reproducible from the method description.

The abstract overstates OOD performance. The 84.4% mAP corresponds to the n=100 sigmoid setting, while CauScale obtains only 18.9% mAP on the n=1000 polynomial OOD setting, where SDCD achieves 29.8%. The claim of 84.4% on out-of-distribution data is therefore misleading.

There are no error bars, standard deviations, or repeated training seeds. Results are averaged over only 5 test graph instances, making it difficult to assess the reliability of the reported gains, especially at large scale.

Scalability and memory claims are not fully supported. The main results report inference time but not peak GPU memory for CauScale at n=500 or n=1000. The AVICI comparison uses a pre-trained checkpoint rather than training on the same data, so the accuracy and speed comparison may not be apples-to-apples.

The reduction unit pools across observation samples that may correspond to different intervention targets. This can mix interventional regimes and destroy regime-specific causal information. The paper provides no analysis or ablation to show this is safe.

No identifiability guarantees or detailed assumptions are discussed. The method is presented as causal discovery, but for many settings (e.g., linear Gaussian with limited interventions) the graph is not identifiable without additional assumptions. The paper does not clarify when the amortized model can recover the true causal structure.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release or working project URL is provided, and several implementation details are missing (e.g., how the prior is computed when the covariance is singular, exact mAP computation for directed edges, baseline tuning protocols).

Presentation has multiple issues: typos and malformed notation (e.g., 'Tesing data', 'DaraGraph', 'd_heal'), inconsistent references, and text that does not always match the tables (e.g., the abstract's OOD claim versus the polynomial n=1000 result).

The decision not to enforce acyclicity is justified by saying 'real-world data sometimes contain cycles.' For standard causal structure learning, cycles usually indicate model misspecification or feedback across time scales, not valid instantaneous causal graphs. Although the paper reports fewer cycles, the justification is weak.

The comparison to recent amortized methods is incomplete. AVICI is not retrained on the same data, SEA is tested mainly with one GIES variant, and DiffAN/FCI are excluded at scale, so the paper does not fully establish state-of-the-art performance against the strongest relevant baselines.

strengths: Targets an important and timely problem — scaling amortized neural causal discovery to large graphs — and demonstrates a concrete architecture that trains on 500-node graphs and performs zero-shot inference on 1000-node graphs, which is a genuine step beyond prior amortized methods.

The efficiency design (sample-dimension reduction unit + tied attention weights) is sensible, and the ablations in Figures 3–5 and Table 2 provide some support that these components improve time/memory without destroying accuracy.

The empirical coverage is broad: linear/NN/sigmoid/polynomial synthetic mechanisms, multiple graph topologies (ER/SF/SBM), and semi-synthetic SERGIO-GRN data, plus dedicated OOD generalization (Fig 6) and sample-size (Fig 7) analyses that are often missing in comparable papers.

The two-stream design with a data2graph message that distills relational evidence before compression is a reasonable way to mitigate information loss from pooling, and the graph-stream ablation (Fig 4) supports its importance.
weaknesses: The central baseline comparison is confounded. AVICI is evaluated with pre-trained checkpoints (scm-v0, neurips-grn) trained on different distributions, while CauScale and SEA are trained on the paper's own data. AVICI's reported near-zero mAP (e.g., 0.2 at n=1000) is implausibly poor relative to its published results and is far more likely an artifact of distribution mismatch than a genuine limitation, so the headline accuracy claims over AVICI are not trustworthy.

The advertised 4x–13,000x speedup is an apples-to-oranges comparison: it pits amortized inference against non-amortized methods (NOTEARS, FCI, SDCD) that must solve a fresh optimization per dataset. The only fair amortized comparisons are far more modest (4x vs AVICI, ~200x vs SEA), so the 13,000x framing is misleading.

No variance or error bars are reported despite the model being stochastic and results averaged only over ~5 graph instances per configuration; the statistical significance of the reported gains is therefore unestablished.

The headline 99.6% mAP is on in-distribution synthetic data generated by the same procedure used for training (largely interpolation). The more informative results — 84.4% OOD and especially 18.9% mAP for the polynomial mechanism at n=1000 — show substantial fragility that is under-emphasized in the abstract and conclusion.

Technical novelty is limited: tied attention is taken directly from Rao et al. (2021), the decomposed prediction head from Lippe et al. (2021), and the two-stream framing closely follows prior amortized work. The one new idea (pooling the data embedding along the sample dimension) is simple, and its justification ("aggregating embeddings across observational samples is generally less destructive") is asserted rather than demonstrated.

Acyclicity is not enforced, justified only by the claim that "real-world data sometimes contain cycles" — SCMs are acyclic by definition, and the reported exactly 0.0% cycles for CauScale is suspicious and unsupported by analysis.

The inverse-covariance graph prior is theoretically questionable at the targeted scale: at n≈1000 with m≈1000 the sample covariance is ill-conditioned, yet no analysis of the prior's reliability or of failure modes is given.

Reproducibility is weak: the project page URL is blank, no code release is stated, training requires ~37 h on 8xH200 GPUs, and hyperparameter/data-generation details are only partially specified (relying on external AVICI/SEA code).

Presentation problems: typos (e.g., "DaraGraph Block" in Figure 2), confusing table headers and the unexplained † marker, and overstatements such as "one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale" given the existence of AVICI and SEA.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and practically relevant problem: scaling amortized neural causal discovery to large graphs (up to 1000 nodes inference, 500 nodes training), where prior work like AVICI runs out of memory.

The architecture is well-motivated and clearly described: a two-stream (data + graph) design, a reduction unit that compresses the sample dimension, and tied attention weights borrowed from Rao et al. (2021) to cut attention-map memory. Section 4.6 provides a concrete analytic efficiency analysis (e.g., 26.64% sample-axis and 38.75% node-axis baseline compute).

Empirical results are strong and broad: comparisons against constraint-based (FCI), score-based (NOTEARS, SDCD), FCM-based (DiffAN), and amortized (AVICI, SEA) baselines, plus CORR/INVCOV references, across synthetic and SERGIO-GRN semi-synthetic data, multiple graph sizes, and several causal mechanisms.

The ablation studies are informative and support the design choices: reduction unit (accuracy/time/memory trade-off), graph prior and graph stream contributions, tied attention vs. vanilla attention, prediction head cyclicity, and pooling strategy.
The efficiency gains are substantial and concretely quantified (4x-13,000x inference speedups; sub-second inference at n=1000), which is a meaningful practical contribution.
The paper includes an honest limitations/impact discussion and a generalization analysis that openly reports sensitivity to OOD noise and mechanism functions.
weaknesses: Comparison fairness for the central baseline is questionable. AVICI was not retrained on the authors' data (due to OOM) and instead used the official pre-trained checkpoints (scm-v0, neurips-grn). Since amortized methods are highly sensitive to training distribution, the reported collapse of AVICI at n=1000 (mAP 0.2-0.9) may reflect a training-distribution mismatch rather than an architectural limitation, inflating the perceived advantage of CauScale. This is the key scalability comparison and deserves a more careful, apples-to-apples setup.

The novelty is incremental over AVICI. The tied-attention mechanism is directly adopted from Rao et al. (2021), and the amortized pretraining framing follows AVICI/SEA. The 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale' claim is overstated given AVICI (2022) and SEA (2025) already do exactly this.

The abstract conflates OOD performance: it reports '84.4% on out-of-distribution data,' but the tables show 84.4% corresponds only to the sigmoid case at n=100, while polynomial at n=100 is 50.3% and n=1000 polynomial is 18.9%. The single headline number is selective and somewhat misleading.

Reproducibility is limited. No code/checkpoint release is indicated (the project-page URL is blank), and the training cost is very high (37 hours on 8 H200 GPUs for stage 1, plus 2.75 and 44 hours for other stages), which makes independent reproduction difficult. The two-stage training strategy also introduces dataset-curation choices that are not fully specified.

The prediction-head ablation is weakly supportive: the reported cyclicity differences (0.0% vs 0.0-0.25%) are marginal, and the claim of 'fewer cycles' is a very small effect. The accuracy claim 'comparable to AVICI prediction head' is also only validated on a restricted subset (n in {10,20,100}).

Presentation issues: several typos and inconsistencies ('DaraGraph Block' in Fig. 2 caption, 'Tesing data', missing project URL), inconsistent citation years (e.g., Spirtes 2000 vs 2013, Dhir et al. listed as 2020/2025, Nazaret et al. missing year), and some notation slips (h^{D->G} dimension usage).

No acyclicity is enforced and identifiability is not discussed beyond standard amortized assumptions; the method relies on the test distribution being close to the training distribution, which the generalization analysis itself shows is a real limitation (notably for OOD noise and mechanisms).

strengths: Addresses an important scalability bottleneck in amortized causal discovery and proposes a concrete neural architecture that combines a sample-dimension reduction unit, tied attention weights, and a two-stream data/graph design.
Provides extensive experiments across synthetic and SERGIO-GRN benchmarks, varying graph sizes (up to n=1000), causal mechanisms, and multiple baselines, with eight evaluation metrics.
Reports strong efficiency gains: 4x–13,000x inference speedups, successful training on 500-node graphs, and inference on 1000-node graphs where AVICI fails due to memory.

Includes useful complexity analyses (FLOP-level time and peak memory proposition) and ablations for the reduction unit, graph prior, graph stream, tied attention, prediction head, and pooling strategy.
Evaluates OOD generalization, latent-confounder robustness, graph-prior sensitivity, and sample-size effects, and includes an honest limitations discussion and impact statement.
weaknesses: Critical implementation detail is missing for the inverse covariance graph prior when the number of samples m is less than or equal to the number of nodes n (e.g., n=1000, m=1000); the empirical covariance is singular, and the paper does not specify regularization or pseudoinverse, undermining reproducibility and validity of the large-scale results.

The abstract and introduction overstate OOD performance by citing 84.4% mAP (sigmoid, n=100) while omitting that polynomial OOD at n=1000 achieves only 18.9% mAP and is worse than SDCD, so claims of uniformly superior accuracy across mechanisms are not supported.

Evaluation is limited to synthetic and semi-synthetic data, with no real-world observational benchmarks, despite motivation from scientific AI and data analysis; this limits demonstrated practical significance.

Baseline comparison may be unfair: AVICI is not retrained on the authors' data due to OOM and instead uses pretrained checkpoints from different distributions, so its failure at n=1000 may partly reflect distribution mismatch rather than architectural limits.
The core data2graph layer is not ablated against alternative summarization designs, so the specific architectural choice is not fully justified.

Several large-scale results have high variance with only 5 test graphs per setting (e.g., n=1000 polynomial mAP 18.9±13.8, SHD 3985±2975), weakening statistical support for the strongest scalability claims.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: typos such as 'Tesing data' and 'focus' instead of 'focuses', reference errors (e.g., Chickering 2002 vs. 2020, Hauser & Bühlmann 2012 vs. 2007), a missing project page URL, and no code link.

The reduction unit lacks a rigorous theoretical justification; average pooling across observations may discard statistical information, and the claim that it preserves structural signals is not formally established.
Cyclicity at n=1000 requires post-hoc cycle-breaking, and for polynomial OOD an average of 103 edges per graph are removed, indicating substantial structural errors that are not deeply analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: scaling amortized causal discovery to large graphs, where time and memory bottlenecks are severe.

Proposes a concrete efficient architecture with a reduction unit for sample-dimension compression and tied attention weights for memory reduction, yielding large inference speedups (e.g., 0.83s vs 10,896s for NOTEARS at n=1000) and lower memory.

Provides extensive experiments: synthetic and SERGIO-GRN benchmarks, multiple mechanisms, OOD settings, ablations on reduction unit, graph prior, graph stream, tied attention, prediction head, and pooling strategy, plus AID metrics and error bars.

Demonstrates practical scaling: training up to 500 nodes and inference up to 1000 nodes, with strong in-distribution accuracy (99.6% mAP on linear n=100) and clear advantages over SEA on synthetic data.
Includes useful robustness analyses (latent confounders, prior quality, sample size) and an appropriate ethical impact statement treating predicted graphs as hypotheses.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction misleadingly claim 84.4% mAP on out-of-distribution data, but this is only the sigmoid n=100 setting; polynomial OOD is 50.3% at n=100 and 18.9% at n=1000, with very high variance (±13.8). The headline overstates OOD performance.

The comparison to AVICI is unfair: AVICI is evaluated only via a pretrained checkpoint because training OOMs, while CauScale is trained on the exact same data distribution. This makes accuracy comparisons (e.g., 99.6 vs 25.9 mAP at n=100) invalid and weakens claims of superiority over prior amortized methods.

The claim that prior work fails at 500-node training due to space limitations is overgeneralized: SEA is trained on the same 150–500 node data for 48 GPU-hours, so 'prior work' does not uniformly fail. The statement should be restricted to AVICI.

The SERGIO-GRN baseline SEA-gies is suspicious: GIES is typically a discrete/categorical estimator, yet it is applied to continuous SERGIO data without a clear discretization protocol. The enormous gap (SEA 5.6 mAP vs CauScale 54.0 mAP) may reflect an unfair baseline setup rather than a true architectural advantage.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is released, and the project page URL is missing ('Our project page is at .'). While hyperparameters and training details are provided, independent verification is hindered.

Novelty is incremental: the method combines existing components (axial attention, tied attention from MSA Transformer, average-pooling reduction, inverse covariance prior). The graph prior is classical and heavily relied upon—ablation shows large degradation without it—so the neural contribution may be less than claimed.
Evaluation is restricted to synthetic and semi-synthetic data; the paper acknowledges this, but no real-world observational dataset is tested, limiting demonstrated practical significance.

The cycle-breaking results at n=1000 show that for polynomial mechanisms an average of 103 edges per graph must be removed, and SHD remains very high (3985 before, 3891.8 after). This undercuts the strong framing of 1000-node scalability for complex mechanisms.

The reduction unit pools embeddings across observational samples, but the data include interventional samples with different intervention targets. Pooling across such regimes may mix interventional and observational information, and this potential failure mode is not analyzed.

The originality claim 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale' is overstated given prior amortized pre-training works such as AVICI and SEA, which are directly compared against.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck: amortized causal discovery at scale. The paper demonstrates training on graphs up to 500 nodes and zero-shot inference on 1000-node graphs, a regime where prior amortized methods (e.g., AVICI) fail with OOM, making the scaling contribution practically meaningful.

The efficiency contribution is well-supported by both theory and measurement. Section 4.6 and Appendix E provide FLOP-level and peak-memory analyses (e.g., 36.6% of baseline sample-axis compute, reduction of attention-map memory from O(RHC^2) to O(HC^2)), which are consistent with the reported 4x-13,000x speedups and reduced GPU memory in Table 1 and Figure 3.

The evaluation is broad and uses a well-chosen metric suite, including eight metrics (SHD, mAP, AUC, OA, Cyclicity, and the AID family from Henckel et al. 2024), across multiple mechanisms (linear, NN, sigmoid, polynomial), graph sizes, and graph families (ER, SF, SBM), with standard deviations reported in Appendix F.2.

Component contributions are disentangled through ablations: the reduction unit (Figure 3), the graph stream and graph prior (Figure 4), tied vs. vanilla attention and the decomposed prediction head (Figure 5), and pooling strategy (Table 3). The paper also reports robustness to latent confounders (Section 5.6) and to noisy graph priors (Section 5.7), which is a thoughtful addition.

The limitations are handled honestly: the paper reports emerging cycles at n=1000, applies and quantifies a cycle-breaking procedure (Table 2), documents OOD degradation (Figure 6), and explicitly states in the conclusion that real-world evaluation is future work.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is materially weakened. The project page URL is left blank ('Our project page is at .'), and no code or model release is mentioned. Combined with a training regime of 37 hours (Stage 1) plus 2.75 hours (Stage 2) on 8 H200 GPUs for synthetic data and 44 hours for SERGIO, independent reproduction is effectively infeasible for most groups.

The AVICI comparison is confounded. AVICI is evaluated using public pre-trained checkpoints (scm-v0, neurips-grn) rather than being retrained on the paper's data, whereas SEA is retrained (48-72 GPU-hours). This asymmetry means the head-to-head accuracy and memory claims against AVICI are not apples-to-apples, yet the paper leans on AVICI's OOM as a key space-efficiency result.

Novelty is largely compositional. Tied attention weights are taken directly from Rao et al. (2021), the reduction unit is average pooling over the sample axis, and the two-stream data/graph design overlaps substantially with prior amortized architectures. The contribution is an effective engineering synthesis rather than a fundamentally new method, and the paper does not articulate a novel theoretical insight.

The near-perfect in-distribution results (99.6% mAP, SHD 15.2 on n=100 linear) may be partly attributable to the informative inverse-covariance prior rho, which for linear Gaussian SCMs already encodes structural information. The graph-prior ablation (Figure 4) shows degradation when removed, but the interaction between prior informativeness and the claimed accuracy is not fully separated from the architecture's own contribution.

There is a potential inconsistency in the SERGIO-GRN setup: Section 5.2 states the training sample size is increased to 5,000, while the results table is labeled 'sample size = 20000.' The training/testing sample-size relationship should be clarified, as it affects interpretation of the GRN results (mAP 54.0 and 39.2 are modest in absolute terms).

The two-stage, size-bucketed training procedure (10-100 then 150-500 nodes) leaves open whether the reported generalization to n=1000 reflects genuine structural extrapolation or is aided by size-grouped batching and zero-padding effects. A controlled analysis of this would strengthen the central scalability claim.

Evaluation is confined to synthetic and semi-synthetic data; no real-world observational benchmark is included, so the practical utility of the method for the motivating scientific applications remains unverified.
